headings.title: Introduction to Intravenous Therapy and Indications
headings.content: Intravenous (IV) therapy is a foundational clinical skill for nursing students in Nigeria and globally, allowing direct administration of fluids, medications, blood products, and total parenteral nutrition into the systemic circulation. The primary indication for IV therapy is the rapid and precise correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances, especially when oral intake is impossible, restricted, or clinically inadequate due to conditions such as severe gastroenteritis, persistent vomiting, or bowel obstruction. Furthermore, IV access is critical in emergency situations for rapid administration of life-saving drugs like adrenaline, anticonvulsants, or emergency antibiotics, guaranteeing immediate bioavailability without waiting for gastrointestinal absorption. It is also routinely used for delivering chemotherapy, general anesthesia, and continuous blood transfusions in surgical and medical wards. As student nurses preparing for professional practice, understanding these clinical indications ensures you can anticipate medical prescriptions and prioritize patient safety. However, because IV therapy bypasses the body's natural physiological barriers, it carries an inherent risk of rapid toxicity or adverse reactions, making careful clinical judgment mandatory before initiation. Nurses must always verify the healthcare provider's prescription, confirm the patient's identity using safe hospital protocols, and evaluate whether the prescribed therapy matches the patient's current clinical diagnosis and fluid status.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of Peripheral Veins
headings.content: A thorough understanding of peripheral vascular anatomy is essential for successful venipuncture and minimizing patient discomfort. The most commonly selected peripheral veins for cannulation are located in the upper extremities, specifically the dorsal venous network of the hand, the cephalic vein, the basilic vein, and the median cubital vein located in the antecubital fossa. When selecting a vein, nursing students should start distally on the upper extremities, saving proximal sites for future cannulation if the vein becomes damaged or infiltrated. Ideal veins should feel soft, spongy, straight, and bouncy upon palpation, whereas sclerosed, hardened, thrombosed, or tortuous veins must be avoided because they increase the risk of infiltration, extravasation, and mechanical phlebitis. The structure of a vein consists of three layers: the tunica intima (innermost endothelial lining), the tunica media (middle muscular and elastic layer), and the tunica adventitia (outer connective tissue layer). Venous valves are also present, especially near bifurcations, and must be taken into account during catheter advancement to prevent trauma. Additionally, nurses should consciously avoid areas of joint flexion, such as the wrist or antecubital fossa, whenever possible, because movement in these areas can easily dislodge the cannula or obstruct the flow of infusion solutions, leading to premature site failure.

headings.title: Equipment, Supplies, and Infusion Solutions
headings.content: Successful initiation of intravenous therapy requires gathering appropriate equipment, sterile supplies, and the correct infusion solutions. Essential supplies include non-sterile gloves, an appropriately sized peripheral IV cannula (commonly 18G to 24G depending on age and clinical purpose), a tourniquet, antiseptic skin cleansing swabs (such as 2% chlorhexidine in 70% isopropyl alcohol), transparent dressing materials, tape, an extension set or infusion tubing, and a flushed saline lock or infusing IV bag. Infusion solutions are categorized based on their tonicity relative to blood plasma: isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic. Isotonic solutions, such as 0.9% Normal Saline and Lactated Ringer's solution, have the same effective osmolality as body fluids and are primarily used for extracellular fluid replacement without causing fluid shifts between compartments. Hypotonic solutions, such as 0.45% Normal Saline, have a lower osmolality and cause fluid to shift out of the intravascular space into the intracellular and interstitial tissues, making them useful for cellular dehydration. Hypertonic solutions, such as 10% Dextrose in Water or 3% Normal Saline, have a higher osmolality, pulling fluid from the cells and tissues into the vascular space, which requires careful monitoring to prevent circulatory overload. As a nursing student, you must always double-check the solution bag for clarity, expiration date, and integrity before hanging it.

headings.title: Patient Assessment and Preparation
headings.content: Comprehensive patient assessment and psychological preparation are critical steps before starting intravenous cannulation. Begin by introducing yourself, verifying the patient's identity using two distinct identifiers, and checking the medical prescription against the patient's identification band. Assess the patient's medical and allergy history, specifically checking for latex, tape, or antiseptic allergies that could trigger adverse reactions during the procedure. Evaluate the patient's developmental age, cognitive status, and emotional readiness; pediatric and anxious adult patients may require reassurance, calm explanations, or distraction techniques. Inspect the upper extremities thoroughly to select the most appropriate vein, keeping in mind contraindications such as an ipsilateral mastectomy, a side with an arteriovenous fistula for dialysis, or a limb with paralysis or severe lymphedema. Preparing the patient also involves explaining the expected mild discomfort of the needle stick and positioning them comfortably with good lighting. Ensure the patient is lying down or seated securely to prevent injury in case of a vasovagal syncope episode during the procedure. Finally, prepare your workspace meticulously by priming your infusion tubing or saline lock to eliminate air bubbles, thereby reducing the critical risk of iatrogenic air embolism during cannulation.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Cannulation
headings.content: Executing a peripheral IV cannulation requires strict adherence to aseptic technique and hand-eye coordination. First, perform meticulous hand hygiene and put on non-sterile gloves. Apply the tourniquet 3 to 4 inches above the chosen venipuncture site to engorge the vein without occluding arterial blood flow. Cleanse the selected site with an antiseptic swab using a friction back-and-forth or concentric circular motion for at least 30 seconds, and allow it to air-dry completely to ensure maximum antimicrobial efficacy. Stabilize the vein by applying gentle traction on the skin distal to the site with your non-dominant hand. Hold the IV cannula with the bevel facing upward at a 15- to 30-degree angle relative to the skin. Insert the needle through the skin and into the vein; a sudden 'flash' of dark red blood in the flashback chamber confirms successful entry into the lumen. Lower the cannula almost parallel to the skin and advance the catheter a few millimeters further to ensure it is fully within the vessel. While stabilizing the hub, gently advance the plastic catheter forward off the needle while withdrawing the stylet simultaneously. Never re-insert the needle into the catheter, as this can shear the plastic tip, causing a catheter embolism. Release the tourniquet, connect the primed extension set or saline lock, secure the device with a sterile transparent dressing, and dispose of sharps immediately in a puncture-proof container.

headings.title: Calculating and Regulating Flow Rates
headings.content: Accurate calculation and regulation of intravenous infusion flow rates are essential nursing responsibilities to prevent fluid overload or under-infusion. Nursing students must master the mathematical formulas used for both gravity-fed infusion sets and electronic infusion pumps. For gravity infusions, the flow rate is measured in drops per minute (gtt/min) and is calculated using the formula: Flow Rate (gtt/min) = [Volume to be infused (mL) × Drop factor (gtt/mL)] ÷ Time in minutes. The drop factor refers to the specific calibration of the infusion tubing set, categorized as macro-drip sets (typically 10, 15, or 20 gtt/mL) for routine adult infusions or micro-drip sets (60 gtt/mL) for pediatric or very precise low-volume infusions. When using an electronic infusion pump, the rate is programmed directly in milliliters per hour (mL/hr). Nurses must regularly monitor the infusion drip chamber or pump display to ensure the fluid is infusing at the prescribed rate. Factors that can alter flow rates include changes in patient position, height of the IV pole, kinking of the tubing, or a partially infiltrated cannula. If the rate drifts, the nurse must recalculate and readjust the roller clamp carefully while maintaining strict aseptic technique around connection ports.

headings.title: Complications of Intravenous Therapy and Prevention
headings.content: Intravenous therapy carries potential local and systemic complications that require vigilant nursing surveillance and prompt intervention. Local complications include infiltration (infusion of fluids into surrounding subcutaneous tissue resulting in swelling and coolness), extravasation (leakage of vesicant medications into tissue causing blistering and necrosis), phlebitis (inflammation of the vein wall characterized by pain, redness, and a palpable cord), and local infection at the insertion site. If phlebitis or infiltration occurs, the nurse must immediately stop the infusion, remove the cannula, elevate the limb, and apply appropriate warm or cold compresses according to facility policy and the type of fluid infused. Systemic complications are more severe and include circulatory fluid overload (manifested by hypertension, dyspnea, and crackles in the lungs), air embolism (caused by air entering the circulatory system, leading to sudden cardiovascular collapse), and catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI), which can lead to sepsis. Prevention relies heavily on practicing strict hand hygiene, maintaining aseptic technique during insertion and dressing changes, changing peripheral sites and dressing materials according to hospital policy (usually every 72 to 96 hours), and continuously monitoring the patient's vital signs and respiratory status.

headings.title: Maintenance, Site Care, and Discontinuation
headings.content: Proper maintenance, ongoing site care, and safe discontinuation of intravenous therapy are vital to prevent infections and vascular trauma. Routine maintenance includes assessing the insertion site every shift for signs of tenderness, erythema, swelling, or exudate. Transparent dressings should be inspected regularly and replaced immediately if they become loose, damp, or soiled, always using sterile technique. Infusion administration sets should be changed per hospital protocol—typically every 24 hours for continuous lipid or blood products, and every 72 to 96 hours for standard crystalloid solutions. Intermittent infusion ports or saline locks must be flushed with normal saline before and after medication administration to maintain patency and prevent clotting. When IV therapy is no longer required or if a complication develops, the nurse must discontinue the device. Discontinuation involves explaining the procedure to the patient, performing hand hygiene, closing the roller clamp, gently removing the dressing and tape while stabilizing the skin, withdrawing the catheter parallel to the skin in a smooth motion, and immediately applying firm pressure with sterile gauze for at least 2 to 3 minutes until bleeding stops. Inspect the removed catheter to ensure the tip is intact, apply a clean adhesive bandage, and document the discontinuation time, site condition, and patient tolerance.
